meta.title: Product Tour
meta.description: A guided tour that survives the real world: a card that reflows to a bottom sheet on phones, a spotlight that tracks its anchor while the page scrolls, steps that can hand control back to the user, and a clear distinction between finishing and giving up.

blocks.content: Guided tours sound simple until you ship one. The card lands off-canvas on a phone. The spotlight lags a frame behind the element it is meant to be highlighting. The anchor for step 4 lives inside a menu that isn't open yet, so the card pins itself to the top-left corner. And the one callback you were given fires whether the user finished the tour or slammed the close button on step one.

This system is built around those failures. Below 640px the floating card becomes a bottom sheet, capped at 60% of the small viewport height so the highlighted element stays visible above it. Anchor measurement is coalesced into one rAF per frame, so the cutout tracks the page instead of chasing it. A step can declare itself interactive and hand the click back to your UI. And completing a tour and abandoning one are different events.

blocks.title: How the spotlight works
blocks.content: A full-screen SVG sits above the page. A white rect covers everything; a black rect the size of the active anchor punches a hole in the mask. The dimmer is painted through that mask, so the anchor is lit without moving in the layout. The mask id is generated per instance — SVG ids are document-global, so a hardcoded one collides the moment two tours exist on a page.
Start the tour and walk through the dashboard. Use ← → to navigate and Esc to close. Narrow your browser below 640px and the card becomes a bottom sheet.

optionalSteps.title: Peer dependencies
optionalSteps.note: Floating placement, overlay transitions, and the asChild prop respectively.

blocks.content: Wrap the subtree you want to tour with TourRoot, define your steps, then mark each target with TourAnchor.

blocks.title: Finishing is not the same as quitting
blocks.content: onComplete fires only when the user reaches the end and confirms. onSkip fires when they close early. onEnd fires for both and receives the reason — "completed", "skipped" or "stopped" — if you would rather handle them in one place.

blocks.title: asChild
blocks.content: Use asChild when the anchor is already an element you control. It merges the anchor props onto your child via Radix Slot rather than wrapping it in an extra div that could disturb your layout.

Below 640px a 320px card pinned to a small anchor has nowhere to flip to, so it stops trying. The card detaches from the anchor and renders as a bottom sheet: full width, rounded top, safe-area aware, and capped at 60svh so whatever is being highlighted stays visible above it. The spotlight cutout keeps working exactly as it does on desktop.

On desktop the card is additionally constrained by the floating-ui size middleware, so a long step on a short window scrolls inside the card instead of overflowing the viewport. Nothing about your step definitions changes — the same steps drive both layouts.

blocks.title: svh, not vh
blocks.content: Mobile browsers shrink the viewport when the URL bar retracts. The sheet is sized in svh (small viewport height) so it does not jump as the bar appears and disappears mid-tour.

A spotlight that dismisses the tour when you click it is working against you — the whole point of highlighting a button is that the user should press it. Mark a step interactive and the dimmer stops intercepting pointer events, so the click reaches your UI. The tour advances when you tell it to.

Half the steps in a real tour point at things behind a closed menu, a collapsed sidebar, or a route that hasn't been visited. Give the step a beforeEnter hook and it runs — awaited, if it's async — before the card is placed.

If the anchor still cannot be found, the card does not pin itself to the top-left corner. It falls back to a centred dialog and reports the situation through isAnchorMissing, so you can log it or skip the step. The anchor is also scrolled into view automatically when it sits outside the viewport — pass scrollToAnchor={false} to opt out.

blocks.title: Step numbers do not have to be contiguous
blocks.content: Steps are sorted by their step value and navigated by position, so numbering them 10, 20, 30 to leave room for later insertions works fine. Each value does need to be unique.

A step can carry an image, a GIF or a video, shown flush to the card's top edge above the title. Videos are muted, looped and playsInline so mobile browsers will actually start them, and the play/pause control is visible on touch rather than waiting for a hover that never comes.

blocks.title: Keep media short
blocks.content: The card caps media at 160px tall. A 3–5 second loop reads as an illustration; anything longer competes with the text beside it for the user's attention.
useTour works anywhere inside TourRoot. Use it to drive the tour from your own UI, or to react to where the user currently is.

blocks.title: Resuming a tour
blocks.content: There is deliberately no built-in persistence — where a user left off belongs in your database or storage, not in the component. Read your own flag and call start() plus goTo(savedStep) on mount.

The card is a labelled dialog. Opening it moves focus inside and Tab is trapped there; closing returns focus to whatever opened the tour. Escape dismisses. ← and → move between steps, and both are ignored while the user is typing in an input, textarea, select or contenteditable — so a tour running over a form does not steal the caret keys.

The page behind stays scrollable on purpose: a tour explains a page, and locking it would make anchors below the fold unreachable. The progress dots are a labelled tablist, the media control is labelled, and every transition collapses to an instant state change under prefers-reduced-motion.

blocks.title: aria-modal is false
blocks.content: The tour card is a dialog but not a modal one — the content it describes has to stay reachable and readable underneath. Screen readers announce the step and its controls without hiding the rest of the page.

items.a: Below 640px the card stops trying to float next to a small anchor and renders as a bottom sheet instead: full width, rounded top corners, capped at 60% of the small viewport height, and padded for the home indicator via env(safe-area-inset-bottom). The spotlight cutout is unchanged, so the highlighted element is still visible above the sheet.

items.q: Does the spotlight keep up when the page scrolls?
items.a: Yes. Anchor measurement runs through a rAF-coalesced tracker rather than calling setState from the scroll handler, and identical frames are skipped entirely — so a fast scroll produces one measurement per frame instead of one React render per scroll event.

items.q: Can the user interact with the thing being highlighted?
items.a: Set interactive: true on that step. The dimmer stops capturing pointer events and clicking the highlighted element no longer dismisses the tour, so you can ask the user to actually perform the action and advance the tour yourself.

items.q: How do I tell finishing apart from quitting?
items.a: onComplete fires only on reaching the end, onSkip only on early exit, and onEnd fires for both with a reason of "completed", "skipped" or "stopped". They are separate callbacks precisely because the analytics question "did onboarding work" depends on the difference.

items.q: The anchor for one of my steps is inside a closed menu. What now?
items.a: Give the step a beforeEnter hook that opens the menu; it is awaited before the card is positioned. If the element is still missing, the card falls back to a centred dialog rather than pinning to the corner, and isAnchorMissing goes true so you can handle it.

items.q: Can I start the tour automatically for new users?
items.a: Pass defaultOpen, or call start() from useTour once you have read your own onboarding flag. Keep the flag in your database or storage rather than expecting the component to remember it.

blocks.title: The anchor no longer draws its own ring
blocks.content: Highlighting is owned entirely by TourOverlay, which draws both the cutout and the ring from a single tracked rect. Anchors only need to be findable and to sit above the dimmer while active.
